summary: Spring Boot auto-configuration automatically configures your Spring application based on the dependencies in your classpath. It uses @EnableAutoConfiguration to scan spring.factories or AutoConfiguration.imports files, applying conditional configurations when specific classes or beans are present.

sections.title: The Interview Answer
sections.content: Spring Boot auto-configuration is the 'magic' that automatically configures your application based on what's in your classpath. When you add spring-boot-starter-web, it automatically configures Tomcat, Spring MVC, and Jackson without you writing any configuration. It works through @EnableAutoConfiguration annotation, which imports auto-configuration classes from META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports file in Spring Boot 3, or spring.factories in Boot 2. These configuration classes use conditional annotations like @ConditionalOnClass to only activate when specific libraries are present. For example, if H2 database is on classpath, DataSourceAutoConfiguration creates a DataSource bean automatically. The key is @ConditionalOnMissingBean—it creates default beans only if you haven't defined your own, so you can always override any auto-configuration by providing your custom bean.

sections.title: Complete Explanation

mistakes.mistake: Thinking auto-configuration is 'magic' that can't be controlled
mistakes.why: Makes developers afraid to customize, leads to workarounds instead of proper overrides
mistakes.correct: Auto-configuration is just @Configuration classes with @ConditionalOnMissingBean. Define your own bean to override any auto-config.

mistakes.mistake: Not checking the auto-configuration report when things don't work
mistakes.why: Wastes time guessing why a bean isn't created instead of seeing exactly which condition failed
mistakes.correct: Run with --debug flag to see Positive/Negative matches and understand exactly why configurations did or didn't apply

mistakes.mistake: Creating duplicate beans that conflict with auto-configured beans
mistakes.why: Causes 'multiple beans of type' errors, confusing when you don't realize auto-config already created one
mistakes.correct: Use @ConditionalOnMissingBean on your custom beans, or exclude the auto-configuration entirely

mistakes.mistake: Disabling ALL auto-configuration because one thing doesn't work
mistakes.why: Loses all the convenience, forces manual configuration of everything
Confusion when migrating Boot 2 to Boot 3, custom starters break
mistakes.correct: Boot 3 uses AutoConfiguration.imports, Boot 2 uses spring.factories. Update your custom starters when migrating.

questions.question: What is @ConditionalOnMissingBean and why is it crucial for auto-configuration?
questions.quickAnswer: Creates bean only if user hasn't defined one. Allows users to override any auto-config by simply defining their own bean.

questions.question: How do you create a custom Spring Boot starter with auto-configuration?
questions.quickAnswer: Create @AutoConfiguration class with conditionals, register in AutoConfiguration.imports, package with spring-boot-starter prefix.

questions.question: What's the difference between spring.factories and AutoConfiguration.imports?
questions.quickAnswer: Boot 2 uses spring.factories with key-value format. Boot 3 simplified to AutoConfiguration.imports with just class names (faster parsing).

questions.question: How do you control the order of auto-configurations?
questions.quickAnswer: Use @AutoConfigureBefore/@AutoConfigureAfter to specify relative ordering between auto-configuration classes.
